segments.title: Why three-star reviews can offer useful criticism
segments.body: Three-star reviews are Alex Clarke's preferred place to look for constructive criticism of books and history videos. A one-word dismissal gives him little he can use to improve the work. Unqualified five-star praise is encouraging, but it can be equally short on specific observations. His preference concerns the usefulness of a review to its creator, rather than a rule that middling ratings are more accurate.

evidence.note: Clarke's personal preference for specific criticism in middling reviews, compared with one-word hostility and unqualified praise.

segments.summary: A preference for middling reviews rests on whether criticism identifies something the author can improve.

segments.title: Is Adept's Path a western or science fiction?
segments.body: Glynn Stewart identifies Adept's Path with a fantasy-western series set in a secondary world. Some readers are convinced the inhabitants arrived in spaceships, an assumption he says he does not understand. The cover's steam trains, bows and apparent wizards prompt Alex Clarke's reaction to its mixture of familiar genre elements. He has not yet read this series during the conversation and describes his usual preference for harder science fiction such as Peacekeepers of Sol.

evidence.note: The question about Adept's Path as a western, Stewart's secondary-world fantasy description and his rejection of an assumed spaceship origin.

segments.summary: The author identifies a secondary-world fantasy western and questions a science-fiction backstory some readers have assumed.
segments.question: Is Adept's Path part of a western series?
segments.answerShort: Stewart calls the series a fantasy western in a secondary world. He does not endorse the readers' assumption that its people arrived on spaceships.

segments.title: Deception and the moral cost of saving a society
segments.body: A military decision can preserve a society and still leave the person carrying it out with a terrible burden. Alex Clarke reads Peacekeepers of Sol through that tension: the protagonist's actions protect his species without erasing the harm he has done. He argues that a good person who reluctantly does something dreadful remains more controllable than someone who enjoys it. Glynn Stewart adds a decisive qualification about his fictional case: the good people were lied to, which secured their cooperation and worsened the trauma afterward.

evidence.note: Clarke's reading of morally damaging decisions and Stewart's clarification that deception secured the fictional participants' cooperation.

segments.summary: Peacekeepers of Sol connects military necessity with deception and lasting moral injury.

segments.title: Book reviews help readers choose, even when authors disagree
segments.body: Glynn Stewart finds praise and criticism making opposite claims about the same character writing. That leaves him unsure what readers expect and unable to write to a single imagined demand. He sometimes checks whether a specific element failed, but generally avoids reviews because he finds negative responses painful and seldom useful. In his view, a review primarily helps another reader decide whether to try the book. Alex Clarke adds that he recognized many early five-star reviewers of his own book from his YouTube audience, so he would not present them as disinterested readers.

evidence.note: Stewart's conflicting character reviews, sensitivity to criticism and reader-audience distinction, followed by Clarke's recognition of supportive existing viewers.

segments.summary: Conflicting reactions to characters and reviews from existing fans complicate the use of ratings as feedback.

segments.title: Comments, ratings and platform visibility
segments.body: YouTube comments can increase visibility even when their wording is hostile, in Alex Clarke's account of audience interaction. He groups comments with likes, shares and subscriptions, including subscriptions made while a particular video is playing. Glynn Stewart describes his impression of Amazon as several overlapping routes to visibility, some involving paid advertising. He believes review volume and average ratings influence the weighting of advertising bids because Amazon wants readers to click and buy.

evidence.note: Clarke's account of YouTube interaction and Stewart's explicitly qualified impressions of Amazon reviews, ratings and paid visibility.

segments.summary: Audience interaction and book reviews can affect recommendations and advertising in the participants' accounts.

segments.title: Separating historical evidence from the author's interpretation
segments.body: A history book contains both evidence and its author's reasoning about that evidence. Alex Clarke tries to distinguish the two by placing evidentiary claims and analysis in separate sentences. He connects writing with the wish to share a story and an interpretation with other people. Glynn Stewart adds the commercial perspective of someone who has made a full-time living from books for a decade: income affects how he assesses the work, even though he says it generally does not determine what he writes.

evidence.note: Clarke's sentence-level separation of evidence and analysis, with Stewart's account of income affecting assessment rather than generally dictating subject choice.

segments.summary: Separate sentences can help readers recognize where historical evidence ends and an author's analysis begins.

segments.title: The calculations behind fictional ship maneuvers
segments.body: Glynn Stewart keeps a notes file for each book alongside a large spreadsheet of mathematics for ship maneuvers. He doubts either editor reads much of the notes beyond the character list. He says neither examines the maneuver spreadsheet, despite the extensive calculations behind the fictional movements.

evidence.note: Stewart's notes, character list and maneuver calculations, with his uncertainty about how much of the notes his editors read.

segments.summary: A maneuver spreadsheet and a separate notes file show how much technical preparation can sit behind a novel.

segments.title: What history is Glynn Stewart reading?
segments.body: Glynn Stewart has recently finished a history of Japanese role-playing games and Andrew Lambert's No More Napoleons. In the games history, he notices a shift from attempting to cover everything toward choosing what the author considers worth emphasizing. The later portion feels faster and less detailed to him, although he still judges the book very good overall. Lambert's book has also helped crystallize some of his thinking, leading into the subsequent conversation about Napoleon.

evidence.note: The two recent reads, Stewart's favorable overall judgment of the games history and his criticism of its compressed later coverage.

segments.summary: Recent reading raises a problem of historical method: how an expanding subject forces an author to select examples.
segments.question: What history books has Glynn Stewart been reading recently?
segments.answerShort: A history of Japanese role-playing games and Andrew Lambert's No More Napoleons. The first made him notice the shift from comprehensive coverage toward selective examples.

segments.title: Why victory at Waterloo would not have saved Napoleon
segments.body: An Anglo-Dutch defeat at Waterloo would only have postponed Napoleon's loss in the counterfactual discussed here. A victory probably required the Prussians to remain absent, leaving them available to regroup with the Russians. The participants also count Austria and Sweden among the forces converging against a France exhausted by years of war. Their argument is that the coalition had already organized against renewed French expansion and could compensate for Napoleon's generalship with overwhelming numbers. British financial support forms part of that wider coalition advantage.

evidence.note: The participants' counterfactual argument about France's exhaustion, coalition armies, overwhelming numbers and British finance.

segments.summary: A counterfactual victory at Waterloo is tested against the coalition forces and resources still available to defeat Napoleon.

segments.title: British subsidies and leverage over allied armies
segments.body: British financial support for allied armies is treated as a source of political leverage after Napoleon's defeat. Glynn Stewart recalls repeated threats to stop sending money when allies resisted British wishes. Alex Clarke estimates that continued support lasted another five or six years and compares the arrangement with American financial influence after the Second World War. The comparison concerns the dependence created by funding an ally, with the speakers drawing their historical starting point from Andrew Lambert's book.

evidence.note: Stewart's recollection of subsidy threats after 1815 and Clarke's approximate duration and comparison with postwar American influence.

segments.summary: Funding allied armies could give Britain influence beyond the campaign that originally brought the coalition together.

segments.title: Fleet Problems and the US Navy's recurring destroyer shortage
segments.body: Albert Nofi's Training the Fleet for War follows the US Navy's interwar Fleet Problems through their objectives, exercise arrangements and results. Its maps allow readers to work through the operations as they follow the development of tactics. A repeated call for more destroyers runs through these exercises. The scale of American destroyer construction during the Second World War gives that recurring demand a later context.

evidence.note: Nofi's exercise-by-exercise structure and maps, recurring destroyer demand and the exchange about wartime construction.

segments.summary: An exercise-by-exercise history traces tactical development and the US Navy's repeated demand for destroyers.

segments.title: Fletcher and Flower: different ideas of a cheap warship
segments.body: The Fletcher-class destroyer is the American benchmark for a cheap warship in this comparison. The Royal Navy's corresponding example is the Flower-class corvette. Those different expectations help explain later procurement arguments, including the Constellation class.

evidence.note: The Fletcher-Flower comparison and its proposed connection to Constellation-class procurement.

segments.summary: A brief Fletcher-Flower comparison links different expectations of an inexpensive ship with later procurement debates.

segments.title: Using Royal Navy Pacific history to teach methodology
segments.body: John McLean's A Mission of Honour covers the Royal Navy in the Pacific from 1769 to 1997. Alex Clarke recalls pairing a passage from that history with a chapter from Peacekeepers of Sol when asked to cover a class at short notice. Students compare the methodologies of the historical account and the fictional treatment. He uses the pairing as a starting point before taking the class to more modern examples.

evidence.note: The named Pacific history, its stated date range and Clarke's account of pairing passages with science fiction before moving to modern cases.

segments.summary: A Pacific naval history and Peacekeepers of Sol become a classroom exercise in comparing methods.

segments.title: Pacific commitments with only a few frigates
segments.body: Britain's Pacific naval commitments could exceed the ships it wanted to keep there in peacetime. A few frigates were expected to carry the reputation of a much larger navy. A crisis such as the Boxer Rebellion could bring substantial reinforcement. Between crises, the small force still had to signal a willingness to defend British territories and, later, friends in the region.

evidence.note: Sparse Pacific deployments, reinforcement in the Boxer Rebellion and the shift from territorial commitments toward supporting friends.

segments.summary: A small peacetime force must represent commitments that depend on reinforcement during a crisis.

segments.title: What would freedom of navigation look like in space?
segments.body: Navigation rights depend on the mechanics of travel in these hypothetical settings. In a twenty-five-year voyage to Alpha Centauri, a detour adds years and supplies constrain the route. Practical wormholes would instead create chokepoints whose owners could exclude unfriendly traffic. Point-to-point travel shifts attention toward the need to stop for fuel, including a possible distinction between protected inner planets and accessible gas giants. The physical parameters are unknown, so the alternative arrangements remain hypothetical.

evidence.note: The navigation question, three hypothetical travel arrangements and explicit uncertainty about future physical parameters.

segments.summary: Travel time, wormholes and refueling stops produce different possibilities for passage through another power's system.
segments.question: What would a freedom-of-navigation cruise look like in space, and would control of a planet give control of its solar system?
segments.answerShort: It depends on how travel works. Slow voyages constrain routes and supplies, wormholes create chokepoints, and point-to-point travel can make access to refueling stops the central issue.

segments.title: Why patrolling Jupiter is harder than patrolling Earth
segments.body: A claim to control a planetary system has to be backed by enough surveillance and patrol capacity to enforce it. Jupiter raises a problem of scale as well as distance from a power's center. Glynn Stewart sketches roughly forty relevant Lagrange points around its larger moons, compared with about four near Earth in his example. He immediately questions how the moons' interactions would affect those positions and their reliability. He explicitly places that multi-body calculation outside his mathematical expertise, leaving the numerical sketch uncertain.

evidence.note: Enforcement costs and Jovian scale, with Stewart's rough Lagrange-point estimate and explicit uncertainty about multi-body interactions.

segments.summary: Jupiter's size and moons complicate patrol coverage, while the proposed orbital positions remain an acknowledged rough sketch.

segments.title: Why maritime precedent may shape future space law
segments.body: Maritime precedent supplies a proposed analogy for activity in space beyond national territory. Alex Clarke characterizes maritime law as largely unwritten and heavily dependent on precedent, using a provocative pair of ninety-percent estimates to express that view. He suggests that its concepts offer a starting point for imagining space law, while both participants acknowledge some existing provisions for space. The Martian provides the fictional illustration: taking over a vessel away from national territory becomes a joke about being a pirate on Mars. He recalls using the analogy to prompt a classroom discussion.

evidence.note: Clarke's broad characterization of maritime precedent, acknowledgment of some space-law provisions and the fictional Martian piracy analogy.

segments.summary: The Martian's piracy joke introduces a discussion of how maritime precedent might inform imagined rules for space.

segments.title: Naval treaty expectations and uncertainty about space weapons
segments.body: Reconnaissance satellites prompt a distinction between military activity in space and armed spacecraft. Glynn Stewart points out that the satellites under discussion are not supposed to be armed, and neither participant claims to know whether they are. Alex Clarke compares that uncertainty with ships built under the Washington and London naval treaties and the gap between expectations and actual compliance. They also recall anti-satellite tests, but Stewart is unsure which country's recent headlines he has in mind and warns that his sense of when they occurred is unreliable.

evidence.note: The distinction between military satellites and armament, uncertainty about whether satellites carry weapons and poorly dated recollections of anti-satellite tests.

segments.summary: A naval-treaty analogy distinguishes stated limits from what the speakers know about actual spacecraft armament.

segments.title: How did Japan influence Glynn Stewart's worldbuilding?
segments.body: Recent travel and reading leave traces in the names Glynn Stewart invents for new star systems. Most names are varied, but a few cluster around something that has recently caught his attention. In the House Adamant series, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries inspires a fictional colony project extending across several systems. Some of those worlds now belong to a cold-war power while others remain independent. Alex Clarke jokes that approved subsidiaries probably still own everything, and Stewart agrees only tentatively.

evidence.note: Stewart's naming habits and fictional Mitsubishi colony project, followed by a tentative joke about continuing subsidiary ownership.

segments.summary: Travel to Japan influences fictional system names and a corporate colony project divided by later politics.
segments.question: Did the trip to Japan influence Glynn Stewart's fiction?
segments.answerShort: Yes. It influenced names and inspired a fictional Mitsubishi Heavy Industries colony project whose systems are divided between a cold-war power and independent worlds.

segments.title: Fiction makes explicit what historians must infer
segments.body: A character's internal struggle can be the main story even when readers expect the battles to take that place. Glynn Stewart describes moving toward that emphasis in his recent fiction. Alex Clarke finds it useful in teaching because a novelist can reveal thoughts directly, whereas a historian has to infer motives from what was written down and what happened. Stewart draws on those historical reconstructions to imagine what people would think in situations he invents. He also corrects the assumption that he reads many autobiographies: he has read some, but Nelson Mandela is the only example he can recall immediately.

evidence.note: Character-centered plotting, historical inference from records and actions, and Stewart's limited autobiographical reading.

segments.summary: Historical interpretation supplies plausible motives for fiction, while novels can expose thoughts that surviving records leave uncertain.

segments.title: Philip Vian's aversion to staff work and why training matters
segments.body: Philip Vian's Action This Day appeals to Alex Clarke for its author's operational adventures and skill at avoiding Admiralty and staff appointments. That aversion to paperwork becomes a professional weakness in his reading of the memoir. At senior rank, Vian faces the task of organizing a staff without having served on one or attended staff college. The example supports the argument for requiring staff education and practical staff experience before wider command. Glynn Stewart connects it with Starship's Mage, where a young captain's staff appointment completes a qualification needed for eventual promotion to commodore, although her short time at captain still delays advancement.

evidence.note: Clarke's account of Vian's avoided staff appointments and Stewart's fictional combination of a staff qualification with a remaining seniority constraint.

segments.summary: Philip Vian's memoir shows the institutional risk of promoting an operationally gifted officer who has little staff experience.

segments.title: Why promotion can be easier to explain than a high decoration
segments.body: Promotions and medals give an armed service ways to reward people it wants to retain. Promotion can be easier to justify outside the service. A high decoration can require more public explanation, particularly if it involves presentation by a monarch or other head of state. That scrutiny can make a promotion more convenient when the service does not want to explain the circumstances widely.

evidence.note: Retention, promotion and the extra public explanation associated with high decorations.

segments.summary: The public explanation required for a high medal can make promotion the more convenient reward.

segments.title: Honorary Marine rank: extra pay and unexpected authority
segments.body: A fictional captain with three medals of valor also holds the honorary rank of colonel of Marines. A planetary garrison commander uses that status to bring her under his authority, so the distinction has an inconvenient consequence for its recipient. Royal Navy officers holding Royal Marines rank provide the historical parallel: the rank supplied additional pay without naval promotion. Repeated crises eventually make both promotion and further medals difficult to keep awarding. The exchange ends with a joke about asking a monarch which titles of nobility remain available.

evidence.note: The fictional captain's medals and honorary Marine authority, Royal Navy extra-pay arrangements and the joking escalation to noble titles.

segments.summary: A fictional Marine colonelcy leads into historical extra-pay arrangements and the limits of repeated rewards.

segments.title: When military fiction echoes recent historical trauma
segments.body: A copy editor asked Glynn Stewart to add a suicide-bombing warning to an upcoming novel. Alex Clarke initially approaches the subject as a familiar feature of modern warfare, especially grey-zone conflict. Stewart then recognizes a more specific reason to have warned this editor: the New York resident had been near the Twin Towers on September 11, 2001. The novel uses aircraft as explosive delivery vehicles, and Stewart accepts that their being uncrewed drones does not remove the disturbing resemblance.

evidence.note: The requested warning, Clarke's initial warfare framing and Stewart's recognition of the editor's September 11 experience and the limits of the uncrewed distinction.

segments.summary: An editor's experience near the Twin Towers changes how the author thinks about warning readers of a fictional aircraft attack.

segments.title: When does a one-way drone become a missile?
segments.body: An uncrewed vehicle carrying explosives into a target raises a problem of terminology. Onboard guidance and propulsion offer possible distinctions between a drone and a missile, but the participants find both difficult to use as firm boundaries. Glynn Stewart associates drones with quadcopters and missiles with rocket or jet propulsion, then explicitly declines to draw a definitive line. Alex Clarke notes the narrowing difference in onboard control and the need to consider what practitioners call the systems. The question remains open in this exchange.

evidence.note: The classification question, possible guidance and propulsion distinctions, Stewart's refusal to draw a firm line and Clarke's practitioner-language point.

segments.summary: Explosive payloads, autonomy and propulsion fail to produce an agreed boundary between a one-way drone and a missile.
segments.question: If an uncrewed drone hits a target with explosives, is it a drone or a missile?
segments.answerShort: The participants do not settle a precise boundary. Propulsion and onboard control suggest differences, but those distinctions are narrowing and practitioner terminology still matters.

segments.title: Starfleet Command: firing arcs and shoot-and-withdraw tactics
segments.body: Star Trek's weapon names lead into Alex Clarke's recollection of Starfleet Command. In the game as he remembers it, torpedoes can reach targets within roughly forty-five degrees of their launcher, while missiles can turn toward a target elsewhere. He therefore favors missile-carrying ships that can launch and move away in a different direction. The opponent then faces the incoming weapons without the launching ship remaining in the same place to fight. Missile shuttles can join that attack in his account. These are remembered game mechanics and tactics, with the exact edition left uncertain.

evidence.note: Clarke's uncertain game-edition recollection, stated torpedo arcs, turning missiles and use of missile shuttles.

segments.summary: Remembered differences between missile maneuvering and torpedo firing arcs support a launch-and-withdraw tactic.
segments.question: Are there missiles in Star Trek?
segments.answerShort: Yes, in some of the books and games. The Starfleet Command example contrasts turning missiles with narrower torpedo firing arcs.

segments.title: Digital distribution and preserving older computer games
segments.body: Digital distribution changes how older computer games can be found and played. Alex Clarke misses buying physical copies in secondhand shops and associates the decline of that market with services such as Steam. Glynn Stewart credits GOG with tracking down old games and making them work on modern computers, tasks players previously had to tackle themselves. A modern-compatible version of Starfleet Command also raises a question of presentation: Clarke accepts its sharper imagery as technically better while still preferring something about the original appearance.

evidence.note: Clarke's recollection of secondhand physical games and changed imagery, with Stewart's account of GOG's older-game compatibility work.

segments.summary: Keeping an old game playable involves distribution, compatibility and choices about preserving its original appearance.

segments.title: Upcoming books and the memory premise of Adept's Path
segments.body: Adept's Path gives its protagonist another person's remembered life. Glynn Stewart qualifies that inheritance: it contains what the other man remembered when he died, with early life already somewhat fuzzy. Those memories belong to the last fully trained master of a skill the protagonist still knows only at novice level. That provides a considerable practical advantage without making two lives in one head easy to manage.

evidence.note: The upcoming-books prompt, Adept's Path's recently published status and the remembered-life inheritance, including fuzzy early memories and the master's skill.

segments.summary: A novice inherits a dead master's remembered experience, including expertise and the limits of the master's own memory.
segments.question: What upcoming books are you most looking forward to?
segments.answerShort: Adept's Path has just appeared. Its fantasy-western protagonist receives the memories of a dead master, bringing expertise to someone still struggling at a novice level.

segments.title: Does the novice or the dead master own the inherited skill?
segments.body: Whether the novice or the older mind possesses the skill remains unresolved here. Glynn Stewart calls the distinction complicated and says the book addresses it. The young man is already bitter and angry, while the older man has greater reasons for anger about the same things. Their shared memories therefore intensify a shared grievance.

evidence.note: The explicit skill-ownership follow-up, Stewart's deliberately withheld resolution and the two characters' related anger.

segments.summary: The author leaves ownership of the inherited skill unresolved while explaining how the two lives compound the character's anger.
segments.question: When the novice receives the master's memories, does he have the skill himself, or does the dead master still have it?
segments.answerShort: Stewart says the distinction is complicated and addressed in the book; he does not resolve it here.

segments.title: Shadow of Mars and the intelligence risk of a stay-behind officer
segments.body: In Shadow of Mars, a fleet withdraws to distract an approaching enemy and protect an evacuation convoy carrying thirty million civilians. Its operations officer is left with the prepared stay-behind force even though she knows the construction plans for the new fleet intended to retake the occupied planet. Her capture would therefore expose unusually sensitive information, and her unwillingness to sit idle under occupation adds to the danger. Alex Clarke argues that she is precisely the sort of officer specialized infantry should drag aboard before the evacuation. Glynn Stewart explains that the fleet's urgent departure protected the convoy, but reversed the intended personnel arrangement: the ambassador left while the operations officer stayed.

evidence.note: The fictional officer's sensitive construction knowledge, inability to remain inactive and the emergency evacuation that exchanged her intended position with the ambassador's.

segments.summary: Protecting a huge evacuation convoy strands an officer whose knowledge of future fleet construction makes capture especially dangerous.

segments.title: Classical heroes and modern demands for moral purity
segments.body: A planned urban-fantasy protagonist combines an unusually strong commitment to doing good with the trauma of a former special-operations soldier. Alex Clarke compares modern expectations of heroic perfection with Greek heroes who could perform heroic deeds while remaining subject to ego and personal failings. Glynn Stewart stresses that his new protagonist is good without being perfect. He has not yet started writing him and expects him to be less rigid than some earlier characters. In those earlier cases, an inability to compromise on moral rules became the character's greatest weakness.

evidence.note: The planned former special-operations protagonist, Clarke's Greek-hero comparison and Stewart's provisional expectations and earlier examples of moral rigidity.

segments.summary: A planned fallible hero prompts a comparison with Greek heroes and with characters whose moral rigidity becomes a weakness.

segments.title: An unauthorized fleet expedition and the civil-military boundary
segments.body: A joking claim that an admiral hijacked his own fleet receives a more specific correction from Glynn Stewart. The fictional fleet did not yet exist: the admiral stole ships awaiting decommissioning and recruited officers and crews who were no longer active. He then took that improvised force beyond the border without orders. The region specifically required government approval for deployment, making authorization central to the objection even though the hulls were about to leave service.

evidence.note: The correction from seizing an existing fleet to stealing decommissioning ships, recruiting inactive personnel and deploying across a border without required approval.

segments.summary: Ships awaiting decommissioning and inactive crews still form an unauthorized expedition when deployed without the required government approval.

segments.title: Trust, loyalty, and the limits of hard-decision cynicism
segments.body: Offering trust can be a way to build loyalty in a society where trust is scarce. Alex Clarke recalls that theme from a passage about Germany, although he cannot remember the exact quotation. Glynn Stewart accepts the idea to a point but finds that readers in his genre often expect a degree of cynicism he considers unrealistic. His own fiction frequently makes the ruthless man who claims to take hard decisions mistaken or villainous. The disagreement concerns what readers will accept as plausible, with Stewart resisting the assumption that cynicism guarantees realism.

evidence.note: An incompletely remembered observation about Germany and trust, followed by Stewart's critique of expected cynicism and his treatment of ruthless fictional figures.

segments.summary: A recalled observation about trust challenges a military-fiction convention that treats ruthless decisions as inherently realistic.

segments.title: Cunningham's simple orders versus overcomplicated command
segments.body: Walking Stick's complex plans provoke Alex Clarke to question how the fictional officer reached high command. He compares the character's multiple converging operations with Andrew Cunningham's ability to give individual forces simple tasks within a busy overall operation. The fictional plans demand more coordination and support than their commander can manage. Glynn Stewart explains that Walking Stick wants to overawe the enemy as well as defeat it. Clarke favors keeping a large fleet concentrated and striking objectives in sequence, so opponents must face its full strength. Stewart adds that the character's dispersed, converging operations also serve the story, and both acknowledge that narrative constraint.

evidence.note: Clarke's criticism of Walking Stick's command and concentration choices, Cunningham's simpler tasks and Stewart's explanation of the character's motives and narrative role.

segments.summary: Cunningham's simple subordinate tasks provide a comparison for fictional operations that become too complex to support.

segments.title: Rommel's infantry writing and the demands of wider command
segments.body: Erwin Rommel's infantry writing receives a strongly favorable assessment from Alex Clarke. He separates that judgment from his much harsher view of Rommel's suitability for wider command. In his assessment, infantry skill does not establish competence in logistics, artillery or armored coordination. The contrast turns on the additional coordination required when command extends beyond an infantry formation.

evidence.note: Clarke's favorable infantry-book judgment and explicitly critical assessment of Rommel's logistics, artillery and armor coordination.

segments.summary: Praise for Rommel's infantry writing accompanies a sharply critical judgment about his competence in logistics and combined-arms command.

segments.title: Unplanned parallels between a fictional officer and Rommel
segments.body: Reading a biography can reveal parallels that a novelist did not deliberately borrow. Glynn Stewart recalls finding several similarities between Rommel and Kyle Roberts after he was already two or three books into writing the character. He gives the example of getting a school girlfriend pregnant and leaving to join the military. This is his recollection of the biographical comparison, with the particular biography left unnamed.

evidence.note: Stewart's recollection of reading an unnamed Rommel biography during the second or third Kyle Roberts book and recognizing unintended personal-history parallels.

segments.summary: A biography of Rommel surprises the novelist with similarities to a character he had already developed.

segments.title: Why checking corrections can leave a finished book unread
segments.body: Glynn Stewart admits that he has not read every completed book he has written. At one point, he worked through the copy editor's corrections by jumping directly to the next change, without reading the whole manuscript again. He now reads along with the copy edit so that he has actually read the finished book. He considers the earlier practice less satisfactory in retrospect.

evidence.note: Stewart's distinction between accepting individual copyediting corrections and reading through the finished book.

segments.summary: Jumping between copyediting corrections can leave the complete text unread, even by its author.

segments.title: How many of Glynn Stewart's novels have audio editions?
segments.body: Most of Glynn Stewart's published novels have audio editions, but he gives the numbers as an estimate from memory. He guesses seventy-seven or seventy-eight out of eighty-three published novels. Exceptions include a Kickstarter fantasy series and a later Teer & Kard book. Further audio production in that series depends on an earlier edition earning back its cost, despite his high opinion of its narrator.

evidence.note: The direct audiobook question, approximate published and audio counts and the decision to withhold a later Teer & Kard audio edition until an earlier one earns out.

segments.summary: An approximate count leads to the practical reason a later volume may never receive an audio edition.
segments.question: How many of Glynn Stewart's novels have come out as audiobooks?
segments.answerShort: Most: he estimates seventy-seven or seventy-eight of eighty-three published novels. Some exceptions depend on whether earlier audio editions recover their production cost.

segments.title: Why specialist history audiobooks are difficult to finance
segments.body: An audiobook budget has to account for narration and the work needed to turn recordings into a finished edition. Glynn Stewart estimates about 9,000 words per finished hour and a minimum of $200 per finished hour for a good narrator. That rate generally includes editing and audio cleanup. In his experience, roughly a thousand audiobook sales cover the cost, though he presents that as his own rule of thumb. Alex Clarke is considering audio editions of self-published histories if their Kindle performance supports the idea. A joke about paying a friend in burgers leaves the same practical problem: someone must still do the editing and cleanup.

evidence.note: Clarke's conditional plans for history audio editions and Stewart's approximate narration, word-rate and cost-recovery figures, including editing and cleanup.

segments.summary: Personal estimates of narration rates, cleanup work and sales needed to recover costs explain the hesitation over history audiobooks.
